utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. I'm sorry for the delay this morning. It appears Judge Thelin will not be able to sit today and possibly not tomorrow, but the other two members of the Chamber will continue to sit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Yesterday we spoke about -- we spoke about what happened to you in Vukovar, as well as what happened when you went to the Vukovar Hospital and then to the barracks and then to Ovcara, and the last thing we discussed was what happened to you when you went to Negoslavci and you were there for three or four days. You said that you were beaten there, and I just have a couple of questions about that, and then what happened to you following that. Who took you from Ovcara to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We left in a military vehicle. There was an officer sitting on one of the front seats, and in the back there were the four of us and a guard who was with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you arrived at Negoslavci and for that three or four days that you were there, who was guarding you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Down in the basement where we were being held we were being guarded by active-duty military police officers of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said whilst you were there you were beaten. Who was -- who was beating you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reservists would come to the basement. Probably local ones. They would come to the basement and beat us. They would even say that we should all be killed and that they would indeed kill all of us anyway. They tried to get us out of the basement; however, the guards, the military policemen told them that they were in charge of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know whether the military police knew that you were being beaten?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. When they were with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who else was detained with you at this place in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day when we arrived we were blindfolded. When we arrived outside that house and when we started leaving the van, or that vehicle, they blindfolded us and took us down to the basement. We had those blindfolds on for that entire day and night. I could sort of peep out of the blindfold, and when I arrived in the basement I realised that there were other detainees there. You could see that some of them were actually seriously wounded and some were even on stretchers. They were moaning and crying for help. There were four of us who arrived, myself, Hrkic, Hajdar Dodaj, the four of us arrived in addition to those prisoners who were already there by the time we arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how many other prisoners were there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think about 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you able to say whether they -- are you able to say what ethnicity those other people were?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were Serbs among those too who were brought there and held there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: After you were in Negoslavci, were you taken to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were taken from Negoslavci to Belgrade, Topcider more specifically. We were held in a local cinema hall inside one of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How long were you in Topcider for?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were there for about a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And after being kept at Topcider, where were you taken from there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Next we were taken to the military investigations prison in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how long were you at the -- that military prison for?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at the military investigations prison for a couple of months.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Then after that were you taken to a prison in Valjevo?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the military investigations prison, we spent a brief while at the central prison in Belgrade, a month, perhaps even less. From there we were taken to Valjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were you kept in a prison at Valjevo?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And is it correct that you were released from prison on the 14th of August, 1992 in a prisoner exchange?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 14th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And whilst you were in custody in Serbia, you were tried and convicted of deserting the JNA and taking part in an armed rebellion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then in 1994 did you -- were you invited by the Croatian police to be interviewed?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was invited to be interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And briefly can you state how long that interview took and how it was taken, how it was recorded?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting took about an hour. And this is how the interview went: I told that person briefly about everything that he wanted to know, and this person, I think, took some notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to read what that interviewer had noted down?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one gave me anything to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did you ever sign any statement that may have been produced as a result of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Before you testified yesterday did you have an opportunity to look at that, those notes that were taken by the interviewer in 1994? Did you have a chance to read them just before you testified?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you read those notes, you would have noticed that there was no discussion about you being at the Vukovar Hospital and then being at Ovcara. Do you have any explanation why that may not have appeared in those notes? I mean, was it discussed or was it not discussed? Can you give us some understanding?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I read that, I just couldn't make any sense of it, because all the important bits were missing and some appeared to have been added later on. One of the additions was that I had spent a day at the Vukovar barracks after I had been captured, which is just not true. And then also there was the statement that we were taken from the Vukovar barracks to Negoslavci, which is another untruth. There are some more names that are mentioned there that I am not familiar with. Therefore, I must say I find the report quite strange.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And then in 1996 did you provide a statement to an investigator from the Tribunal in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you agree with me that that statement was taken over a two-day period?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you read that statement and then you signed it as being true and accurate at the end of that interview process?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then is it also correct that in 1998 you testified at the Tribunal in the Dokmanovic trial?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I just have a few last questions now, and I'd just like to go back to when you were taken from Negoslavci to Topcider. How were you treated at Topcider?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Topcider it was horrendous. That is where the whole thing began, after Negoslavci, of course. We were forced to write statements, they gave us pen and paper, and we had to write dozens, not to say hundreds of statements. All they wanted to know about was how many people each of us had killed and what sort of crimes we had committed. That was all they were after. Since I hadn't committed any crime or anything at all, of course I was in no position to report any of my own crimes. I told it like it was, but they weren't happy with that, and they applied constant pressure on us to make confessions that just weren't true. Soldiers would go in and out as they pleased. Drunk soldiers, beating us whenever they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Before you testified at your trial in Belgrade for armed rebellion and desertion, about how many times, if you can approximate, were you beaten from the time that you left -- from the time that you arrived at Negoslavci to your time at Topcider until the time that you testified in your own trial in 1992, about how many times were you beaten before you testified, if you can give us an estimation?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many times exactly. Two or three times a day, I'm talking about serious beatings, and just being hit occasionally. That went on and on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And my last question, your trial was in March, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Zlogledja, good morning to you. I am attorney-at-law Vladimir Domazet, one of Mr. Mrksic's Defence counsel. I will be asking you questions on behalf of Mr. Mrksic's Defence team. I'll start with what you have just been telling us about. I'll start with your time in the military investigations prison, the proceedings against you and the court's ruling, your conviction. You have been answering questions by Mr. Smith. You said you spent some time at Topcider, after which you were transferred to the military investigations prison, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In the documents we received from the Prosecution having to do with the indictment and the judgement, it says that you spent in detention the time from the 9th of December, 1991 onwards. This information included in the indictment and the judgement, is it correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you spoke about these proceedings you used plural, saying "we." I suppose that what you had in mind is that Dodaj Hajdar and you stood trial together; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you were co-indictees in the same trial from beginning until it was concluded; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now that we have touched upon him, let me ask you this: Based on what you said yesterday it seems that you were together with him throughout the entire time, both when leaving the JNA, when staying in Vukovar, and then in the hospital, and then at Ovcara and Negoslavci, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you separate from him at some point in time, or were you indeed together through all of these events?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not together through all of these events. We just fled together from the JNA, and then the period that we spent in the Vukovar police we were together then. And later on we separated and met up again in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. We will get to that. But let us begin from that period of time. After the hospital, you were together at Ovcara and did not separate from then on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You were taken to Negoslavci together and were there together throughout?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And finally you were taken together to Belgrade, to Topcider?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You probably remember the charges that the military prosecutor put forward against you. There were three crimes: Deserting the JNA on your own initiative; then the second one was unlawful possession of weapons; and the third one was armed rebellion. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you have a lawyer in that trial?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is it true that you had, in fact, as many as two defence counsel, Mr. Nikola Barovic and Mr. Slobodan Tomic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the two of them and then another lady who was court-appointed, so I had a total of three.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you have Zorica Petronijevic-Gajic in mind?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So she was first appointed by the court and then two lawyers from Belgrade were engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, but this lady was appointed by court and she remained as defence counsel for Dodaj Hajdar, who did not have counsel retained by him.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And then in addition to her you also had these two lawyers who were retained by you and your family and paid by you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now that we're dealing with this trial, do you remember that in the statement mentioned here given to the OTP investigators you said that during the trial you managed to contact your family via your lawyer to tell them that you were alive. Do you remember saying this to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is it also true that your mother came to Belgrade, came to visit you and attended the trial?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You described to us today what you experienced in Topcider. I would like to know whether this trial before the military court was done in accordance with the then regulations in force and does this also apply to the investigations stage?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the military court in Belgrade, we were abused by the guards. We were beaten by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were you personally beaten or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you tell this to your lawyers, Mr. Barovic and Mr. Tomic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did they do anything about it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said they would do everything needed about it to ensure that this wouldn't happen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did this happen again afterwards?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did, but not as often.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you state this in court, be it in the presence of the investigative judge or the trial chamber, did you say anything to them about it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody asked me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Didn't you think it was needed to voice this in your defence? Didn't you think it was necessary to mention this just like you thought it was necessary to say it to Mr. Smith today?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the prison warden toured the facility, and whenever he saw people with bruises he would ask them kindly about the origin of it. So what do you think we dared tell him? We told him that we slipped and fell and hit ourselves. He knew very well what this was all about, but he only laughed about it. So there was no point in telling anything to anyone. Because it would only produce worse conditions for us if we talked about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about the prison warden; I asked you about the trial chamber. This trial was a public one. You had two lawyers retained by you. Did you mention this to the trial chamber ever?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Sometime in September of 1991 you decided to desert the JNA and to flee. Did you then consider that there would be legal implications and that later on you could be charged with very serious crimes as, in fact, did happen?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that. I wasn't thinking about that at all. My only goal was to get away, to flee. We just wanted to go back to our homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. We will go back to that period of time. This was when you reached the positions between Negoslavci and Luzac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that your unit was deployed to a certain area, held positions there, that there were tanks and armoured vehicles there. And there were about 100 of -- soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were those the only positions that you ever held with your unit in that part of the front?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I am concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you have any idea how far that area was from Vukovar itself?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The closest settlement to that field was the suburb of Vukovar, known as Luzac. And the downtown area of Vukovar was quite far away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Between that location and the town -- or rather, could one see the town from there, or were there any woods or hills that would obstruct your view?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were flat-lands, just cornfields.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But in view of this considerable distance, tell us, could one see the town from that area?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the outskirts, but not the centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember how many days you stayed there on those positions before you decided to flee?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A couple of days, perhaps four to five.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, that's what you mentioned in your earlier statements. That's why I asked you this. If I were to tell you that your mate, Dodaj, told you -- told us that you spent 24 days in those positions, what would you say who was right, he or you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am right as concerns these positions. But prior to that, near Negoslavci and in that axis, we spent some 20 days there. And then when we reached these positions then we spent a couple of days there, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, but those were the only positions that you were at from the beginning until you left the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Throughout that time while you were on the positions, did you fire a single bullet? I assume that you had your own personal weapon.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you please qualify this answer. Was this yes, I had a weapon; or yes, I fired from it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a weapon, and at one point I also fired from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember when you fired from the weapon?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shooting started out of the blue. We just heard there is an attack coming, everybody into trenches. There were four or five soldiers there shooting, and then they asked me, well, why weren't you shooting? And that out of fear I had to start firing myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember what soldiers were with you on that occasion? Was Dodaj among them?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't with me in that trench. Nor -- or rather, these soldiers were a mixed group from various units. I didn't even know some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. So that was the single situation of that nature, and you fired randomly. You didn't even know whether there was an actual attack in progress?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: While you were there on the positions, was there an attack on your positions from artillery pieces or some other weaponry?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Had there been any, you probably would have remembered that as something quite distinct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember whether one of your commanding officers was wounded at some point in time? I think that this involved a captain.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in the positions where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And you didn't hear anything of this sort while you were there. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I heard that somebody had been wounded, that a shell had fallen and possibly, as you said, an officer was wounded. But I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You told us who were the people that you discussed fleeing with, and I would like to know whether you were with those people together in order to implement this. You just told us that Dodaj wasn't with you, although he had fled with you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't with me in that trench. Not in that specific area, although we were together in that general area. So after lunch, for example, or whenever everybody gathered at some location, we would see each other. So we got together then, we discussed the situation, we concluded that the war had begun and that we would be forced to take part in the attack against Vukovar. Since we were Croats, the other one was an Albanian and the fourth one was a Muslim, we didn't want to take part in that attack and so we decided to flee.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You say the idea was for all of you to just go home, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But that wasn't where you headed, was it? And you didn't go to the Marinci where Duhanaj was from. You went back to Vukovar, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would it not have been less dangerous and just as possible to head in a different direction, if indeed you wanted to go home. You should have gone elsewhere and tried to discard your uniforms and weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not familiar with the area, we had no idea where to go. Lorenc was the only one who knew the area, knew his way around, and he said the simplest and nearest thing would be to go to Luzac, that suburb of Vukovar, where he had relatives, that these relatives would then take us to the centre of Vukovar and that we would be taken back to our homes from there on. And that was the only thing we could do, because none of us were actually familiar with the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that mean he was assuming that you could go in and out of Vukovar at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he was assuming. It was our own personal responsibility, come what may.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I think his family lived in Marinci, which is near Vinkovci; that was an area in Croatia where there were no combat operations at the time. Wouldn't it have been logical for him, who knew his way around, to try and take you there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should ask him. You should ask him that. I don't know. I didn't know what to do. All I wanted was to go back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. Was there an agreement or did you just set out on that day without any previous agreement with anyone on the other side?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were making plans. We spent about one or two days hatching plans. There were other Croats there from Osijek and Slavonski Brod. We were all caught in that situation. There were five of us who decided to try and escape, and that was our final decision. Some didn't have the courage to go, so they decided to stay behind. We didn't seize our opportunity on that day and then we said well, come hell or high tide.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You crossed the cornfield, you reached Vukovar, and you went straight to the police station, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What happened with your weapons and uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived in Luzac, the Vukovar suburb, he really tracked down this relative of his who gave us some civilian clothes. We changed right there, we discarded our JNA uniforms and put on some civilian clothes, and this man then took us to the Vukovar police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did I get this right: Nobody arrested you, just because you were wearing those uniforms. You -- you changed at this relative's place, and then he took you all the way to the police station at civilians, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And what happened to your weapons? Were you still carrying or had you left it behind somewhere?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we left that behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What happened at the police station? How long were you there for? You say you were vetted. Does that mean that you had to be there under surveillance until they were finished vetting you, as it were?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You might call that several days' detention, actually, until we were thoroughly checked, until they found out who we were and what we were there for.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What were you told then?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They allowed us to call our families.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. You have explained that. You called your aunt in Zagreb. That same day that you were brought to the police station, do you remember another group of soldiers coming?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that same day. But several days later it is indeed true that two other soldiers were brought in, soldiers we knew from our previous area. Allegedly these men had been captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Why do you say allegedly captured? Were you told that they were captured or not?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't say. They didn't make it clear whether they had escaped by accident or had been captured. They were brought in as detainees, that much is certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Who were those two men?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Petar Kuscevic and a Muslim named Rasid.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: How were they treated? The same as you or different?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same. When they were captured they probably said they were Croats, and we confirmed that they were from the same unit. They were checked, just like we were, they spent some time in detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You spoke about your role after the checks. You performed some auxiliary tasks, I think that was the expression you used, and then the going got tough, I think that was the expression you used. In relation to the fall of Vukovar, can you remember when exactly this was that you actively joined the work of the police forces?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the last 20 days or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were you already in possession of a weapon, you personally and those who were with you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not for as long as we were at the police station. Until we were sent to the front line to go and help out. We were given weapons and ammunition at this point, but not before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The same weapons that you had brought with you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: How do you know? The make, the type of the weapon?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the type of the weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know what became of the weapons that you brought on you when you reached the police station?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I do assume that you gave a statement when you arrived at the police station telling them that you came with a weapon or that you had left it somewhere. I suppose one of them might have wanted to pick that weapon up at some point, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We told them that we'd left our weapons there, and then probably somebody did go to fetch it later on. The police or someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were you given police uniforms at the time, and were you actually using those?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Police reserve uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You've mentioned that 20 days before the fall of Vukovar and you said you had to go to the front line. As for you personally, which section of the front line did you go to?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could tell, it was near Luzac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You were saying also that several days before the fall of Vukovar people were talking and some people were in favour of trying to escape. Did you perhaps know at the time that Vukovar's commander left the command and left Vukovar altogether on those very days?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was this communicated to you, was there anything official that you were told, or did you just find out in a different way?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police command was in a basement somewhere. When we arrived there, three groups were set up for what was referred to a break-through but really amounted to an escape. The commander gathered up his 10 active-duty police officers; that was the first group. There was another group, and I myself was a member of that third group that was set to attempt an escape. The first group pulled it off, but the second group and the third group, my own, failed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You have explained, I believe, that your group decided to go back because one of your own had been injured by a mine, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Where exactly did this happen?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We tried several times later on with small groups to escape, to get out. And then this happened. I think it was near the Vuka River, as far as I could tell. He stepped on a mine and it blew his foot to pieces, so we had to take him back to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So this entire area that you were passing through was still not JNA-controlled, since people were still being injured by mines?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He probably stepped on one of our own mines, because we had no idea about the Croatian minefields or where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: "One of our own," you mean a mine laid by the Croatian defenders to block areas from which they were expecting an attack. And what you're trying to say is that you yourselves were not aware of the exact positions of those minefields, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In addition to this injured person, who else was with you on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lorenc Duhanaj was the only one I knew, but there were some other people there, just that I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What about Dodaj Hajdar?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he was with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you meet up with him later on?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all met at the hospital later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say "we all," who exactly do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hajdar, Hrkic, myself. Those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, Dodaj was not with you, nor was Hrkic when this man was wounded. You only saw them later on once you had reached the hospital, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were you carrying a weapon or wearing a uniform by the time you reached the hospital? Can you tell us that, please?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I reached the hospital, I was wearing civilian clothes. I'd had a change of clothes, I had discarded my uniform, and by the time I reached the hospital I was wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Had you put on civilian clothes before you set out to try and escape?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That means you must have stopped off somewhere between that place your friend was wounded and the hospital. You had to get a change of clothes somewhere?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We left him at the hospital and then I went back to get a change of clothes, after which I again went back to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand now how this happened. You were wearing a uniform and, I suppose, carrying a weapon when you left him at the hospital; but then you went back, you got a change of clothes, and you returned to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did all of this happen on the same day?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean did I get a change of clothes on the same day or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: It's just for the transcript and for the sake of the interpretation, if you could please just make a brief pause after each of my questions and I will do the same after your answers. Let me repeat this just to make it clear. You arrived at the hospital, you left Lorenc there; he had been wounded. You were wearing a uniform and carrying a weapon. You went back to get a change of clothes, you changed into civilian clothes, and then went back to the hospital. My question is: Did all of this happen within the space of just a single day or later on?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't on that day; it was that night or evening, if you like. It was the next day that I came back to the hospital wearing civilian clothes. And we had left him at the hospital the previous evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You explained about the change of clothes, but what did you do with your weapon?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply threw it away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was that then the second time you went to the hospital? And where did you get rid of your clothes, where did you throw them away?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, I think that there was a container close by and that I threw the clothes in the container.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say that the container was close by, do you mean that it was close to the hospital? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know where Dodaj left his weapon?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You weren't there, he wasn't with you at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I would just like to make sure that the answer was clear. It says "no," but actually what you were confirming is that you don't know where he threw the weapon away because you were not with him at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you questions about the time you were at the hospital; my colleagues are going to deal with that. I'm going to move on to what you described when you came to the barracks in the buses. Do you remember that you talked about that yesterday, and of course prior to that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: My first question is: Yesterday I think in your answer you said that except for the driver there was another person in uniform who you thought was a military policeman; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you still stand by that answer, that that's how it was?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, an armed driver wearing a JNA uniform and a military policeman, armed. A guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The bus, who else was in the bus that you knew?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hajdar Dodaj was in that bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What about Kuscevic and Hrkic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in another bus in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that there were insults hurled at you at that place by people who were going around, moving around the bus. I assume that that is something that you heard through the glass, through the windows. I assume that this is something that you observed while the buses were standing in front of the barracks. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard what they were saying, but they were also coming in through the front door of the bus that was open. So I heard it also in the bus when they were saying that they were going to kill us and so on and insulted us. They came in the bus, they were beating the people who were sitting in the front seats of the bus, and they were saying, "We are going to kill you all."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The person who was guarding the bus that you mentioned, did he allow those persons to come into the bus or was he preventing them from doing so?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't preventing anyone from coming in. He himself, when he had the opportunity -- well, actually, no, he was also beating the people up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But nobody actually reached you in the bus, they were not able to do so; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could have reached me. I was sitting towards the back of the bus, all the way in the back of the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because there were statements from witnesses who did say that nobody was allowed to enter the bus.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am talking about my bus, that was how it was. I don't know about other buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that at one point in time somebody came in and called out certain number of persons, and I think you said that only one man was called out from your bus; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And you said that you think that that man was from Zagreb. How do you know that? Do you know who this person was?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know his name, but I know that the man tried to defend himself, that he was recognised by a local man for having fired at his tank. I heard him, he was immediately in front of me, and he was saying, "It's not me, I'm from the Zagreb, I'm not from around here at all." But in any case, they did come to get him and they brought him out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: His name was read out from a list, his last name appeared on that list; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no list that was read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was that the only person who was called out and who left the bus?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the only person taken out from my bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In 1998 you gave a statement, and you confirmed that today, for the Dokmanovic case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: On page 649 of the transcript from that trial you said that four to five people were taken out from your bus. How is it possible to have this discrepancy?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now that we're talking about that, it's possible, because when we came to Ovcara, before we reached Ovcara, that's when soldiers entered the bus and they asked if there were any Albanians on the bus, or Siptars. The people who were Albanian stood up and a couple of them were taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We've already heard about Ovcara and we will come to that. I think that that was not the -- we will discuss this a little bit later. The buses left the barracks and, as you explained yesterday, you didn't know that it was Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, could you please wait until the end, because that way we will have everything in the transcript. So you came to an area, the buses stopped there, you saw the hangar there, and much later you heard that this was actually the location of Ovcara; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: According to your statement you were in -- inside one of the last buses, or the buses that were at the back of the column; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When your bus stopped, all the buses that had left at the same time as yours from the barracks were in front of your bus; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If, let's say this was the fourth bus in the line of -- it is said that that was the fourth out of a total of five buses and it was towards the back of the line, can we agree that that was at least 150 metres or more from the place where the people were coming out of the first buses at the front?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the people disembarked from the bus, the bus would drive off, and then the next bus would come. The buses were aligned -- lined up one behind the other. There was no space between the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, but you were in the line until the bus ahead would leave, so you were -- you would then move, you were aware of what was going on. When did you notice Hrkic and Kuscevic, who you said were in the front buses, I assume that they were in the bus in front of yours?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it was our bus's turn, and we were supposed to go out, the people in the front of the bus began to leave the bus, we were at the back, and as we were going out we could see Kuscevic and Hrkic to the side, waiting for us from the side with an officer, and they were even pointing at the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you saw the two of them and an officer standing next to them. Just one officer or more?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one was standing there at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Who was that officer in relation to the ones that you described yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who he was. I don't know his name. I said that he was middle-aged, but I really couldn't tell you definitely who it was. I couldn't give you his first and last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned that when you left the bus you spoke with an officer for a long time. You even said that it was for about 40 minutes. Is that the same officer who was waiting for you whom you talked with first?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not a conversation with an officer lasting 40 minutes. That is our stay in Ovcara before we were taken off to Negoslavci. We talked and then we were free. When the soldiers -- when they thought we were JNA soldiers that were captured, then we weren't allowed to walk around.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you were allowed to be there and wait freely for what was coming next?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was it to the left or the right of the hangar that you were standing?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean where we were standing when we left the bus? The hangar was to the right, the entrance was to the right, and we were standing a little bit off to the left side. We could look at the open door, and we could look and see inside the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: On the other side of the road where the buses were going or were you standing on the same side of the road?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a very narrow, small road, and we were standing to the right side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned first that this officer who was standing with Hrkic and Kuscevic talked with you and you probably, the two of you, confirmed that you were JNA soldiers who were captured. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: How long did you stand there with him and speak with him? You said that this did not last for 40 minutes, 40 minutes was the total amount of time that you spent there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He asked us which unit we were from, which military post number we were from, who was the officer. That was the conversation, in brief. It was a short conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you see other officers there at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was another group of three or four officers a little bit off further down in relation to where this officer was standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And did you speak with any of those other officers?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The four of us stood off separately and a couple of regular JNA soldiers came up to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, you described that yesterday. They offered you cigarettes and they spoke with you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you didn't speak with any other officers other than this one officer before you left?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Which of the officers did you go in the jeep to Negoslavci? Was that the same one that you talked to or someone else?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one that we talked with was, I think, the one who entered the vehicle and that he went to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, that was my question. You think that it was him, that he went with you and that he took you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would suggest that we go on our first break now, if it's a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will have the first break now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much. May I just deal with one small matter of housekeeping, and it is not bad news in any way at all, so Your Honour can rest easy. Your Honour, next Monday Mr. Grujic returns. My learned friend Mr. Lukic, I think, has indicated that he may take two, two and a half hours in cross-examination for him. We have a protected witness coming then, he comes in this weekend for proofing, that's 002. I would have thought that he will take the 13th and the 14th for his evidence, perhaps a little of the 15th. I would not anticipate it would take a long time in chief, myself. We are able to commence Theunens on the 15th, so the Court is aware of that. However, and in fairness to my learned friends, they have always worked on the basis that Theunens would start on the 19th as indeed Your Honour has already indicated it will be two days Theunens, then Kostovic, and two days Pringle. That would mean then that matters should conclude on Friday, the 23rd. The problem, if it be a problem, is that clearly the 15th and 16th are days where we do not have witnesses. We have experts, they are not able to come except for these days. And for my part, it's entirely a matter for the Court, we would not seek to commence calling Theunens on the 15th or 16th, unless the Court wished, but it is available if needs be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. If it is the position that it is convenient to Defence counsel and their experts for Mr. Theunens to start earlier than presently planned, if that could be indicated it would enable us to have just a little more time with each of those expert witnesses. But if that is not convenient in view of the arrangements you've had in place, well then, we will remain with the present plan for the witness Kostovic and the two experts to be in that one week when, as I understand it, Defence experts are here. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm afraid that I cannot give you a final confirmation. I still haven't finalised my arrangements with our expert. We don't know if he can come on the 15th or 16th. I will try to find this out by the end of the week, and I will then inform the Trial Chamber. In accordance with our previous arrangements, I scheduled him for the 19th. There is another matter. I think that my learned friend, Mr. Lukic, when we discussed this last time in the courtroom, mentioned another matter; namely, that the Defence needs some time to study the report of Mr. Theunens, which is several hundred pages long. This is in compliance with the earlier ruling of the Trial Chamber, and this is why we thought that we would need all the time remaining until the 19th. It seems to me that Mr. Moore originally wanted to call Mr. Kostovic and then the military experts were to follow. Has this been changed, or is this still valid? It seems that based on what we heard, Kostovic could cover precisely this period of time, Thursday and Friday, the 15th and 16th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At the moment Mr. Kostovic is planned for Wednesday of that week, with Mr. Theunens the Monday and Tuesday, and Mr. Pringle the Thursday and Friday. It was hoped, though, that Mr. Kostovic would take less than a day so as to allow a little more room. I'm sure if it is the case that a witness such as Mr. Kostovic can be got here for the two days of the preceding week, well then, it could be fitted in, but I see from Mr. Moore that that is not possible. So he remains where he is. It's being left entirely in the hands of Defence counsel whether they are willing to have Theunens start on the Thursday and Friday of the preceding week. If that is not feasible, no pressure, we will start him on the Monday, and the evidence will be from the 19th to the 23rd of the two experts and Kostovic. So it's only if it suits your convenience that we would move Theunens earlier. But, if it's possible to learn by the end of tomorrow, the end of sitting tomorrow, it would obviously facilitate everybody's arrangements. All right? Thank you then. Well, thank you, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, I'm sorry, I thought you were ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to hear the final schedule today, because last time when we discussed this I invested certain efforts aimed at ensuring that my expert arrives here on the 18th, so that he is ready for the courtroom on the 19th. Thursday and Friday is not a problem for me if Mr. Theunens testifies because my expert doesn't need to be here necessarily, but it seems now that even Monday is uncertain. Or rather, for Pringle Thursday and Friday. If Kostovic comes on Monday, that means that we have to reschedule everything once again. I was prepared to accept your earlier suggestion and this is now a new element. So as far as we are concerned, Theunens can begin on Thursday and Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. Can I make it clear the present programme, which will remain in place unless all Defence counsel are in agreement to it changing, the present programme is for Monday and Tuesday, the 19th and 20th, Theunens. Wednesday, or hopefully part of Wednesday, the 21st, Kostovic. Thursday and Friday, the 22nd and 23rd, Pringle. That's the programme. And that would mean the end of the Prosecution case on the 23rd of June. So if there is agreement by tomorrow evening we can hear of it - by the cessation of our sitting at 1.45 tomorrow, not tomorrow evening - we can let Mr. Moore arrange for Mr. Theunens to come earlier, but if that is not convenient to Defence counsel, the programme that I have just mentioned remains the programme. All clear? Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Crystal clear, all of it. I do wish to take advantage of Mr. Moore's presence for something else. What I have in mind is his proposal about our witnesses' statements. In your ruling you say that written submissions should be filed by Friday. I talked to Mr. Moore and it seems logical to us to wait for his motion and then to file a response. I don't know if we should start writing our own motion before we know what the OTP's position is on that. So could the Chamber please issue a ruling in relation to that? This is very important for our timing. Mr. Moore told me yesterday that he was going to tender another 20 documents as exhibits, and he will be moving for that. So I was just wondering if we could have a clear ruling from the Trial Chamber on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If and when the Trial Chamber learns what this is all about, a ruling may be possible. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. The -- dealing with the last point, there are certain exhibits in the 65 ter list which we will submit should go before the Court to be tendered from the bar table. There are not very many. I think actually there could only be perhaps 10 exhibits. There are interviews by these defendants in Belgrade, and they can be distinguished into what are called statements and interviews. They were compiled in 1998; I believe in March and in December. We will be submitting that at the very least the statements made by these defendants should be -- or are admissable and should therefore go before the Court. I have spoken to my learned friend Mr. Lukic about it. I thought I had mentioned it to the court in slightly elliptical terms, because I wanted to speak to and clarify with Mr. Lukic exactly the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber is aware only that there is some discussion between counsel over whether or not these are admissable and that it may become an issue for decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. And the question that we were asking ourselves was whether it can be done orally or whether it can be done written form. In my submission, it's better if it's done in written form. And I was not aware there was any timetable for, as it were, tomorrow evening, because, quite simply, it is not a simple issue, but we certainly could have it before the Court by Monday at midday. That is the only other issue that there is. That we would submit that these which are official records, official transcripts of interviews that they go before the Court as evidence. But there is no great problem with regard to time, as far as I can see. I see Mr. Lukic is nodding in agreement with that. It is the case of whether they are admissable or whether they are not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: By the sound of it, Mr. Lukic is right in thinking that there will be need for a ruling. There will be a decision given as to whether these documents are admitted into evidence or not, but that will only be made when we've either had written submissions from all parties, or oral. And it would seem better if they were written. Mr. Moore has indicated Monday at 12.00 for his submissions. And the question is by what time it would be convenient for the Defence to have their answering submissions. Wednesday, I wonder?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would be grateful, as we shall be sitting on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday for the whole day, and Mr. Moore has just indicated that this is a crucial topic, to have a dead-line for Friday. I believe all three teams will have to confer to reach some sort of conclusion on this. And I believe I have a pretty clear idea already of what Mr. Moore's motion is going to be about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Monday, midday, Mr. Moore, for your written submissions and a motion, if it's a formal motion. Friday, midday for the three Defence teams' responses. That probably means Friday 11.00 a.m. for the decision. No, that can't be right, can it. If you want instant answers out of the Chamber, we will give it attention as soon as we can after receiving the written submissions. Very well. We can now continue. I'm sorry to have kept you waiting. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zlogledja, let us please continue. You remembered the situation faced by the four of you there. You were standing there talking to that officer. After that you were with some other soldiers awaiting transportation. That vehicle and that officer who you left with about 40 minutes later. You said you saw a handful of other officers standing nearby. My question now is in relation to something you said yesterday in answer to one of the questions that were asked about your own 1996 statement to the OTP investigators. You say that the investigators showed you several photographs from a set. You do remember saying that yesterday, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: While looking at these photographs, you first told the OTP that you believed that one of the officers in a photograph was a person you assumed to be some sort of a commander. It wasn't before later on that you were told that this person was General Panic, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Likewise you saw photographs of a person who you said rang a bell. You were later told that this person was Colonel Mrksic. You said the name had a familiar ring to it, but you didn't remember hearing the name in Vukovar. Is that a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you looked at some photographs from this set, and these persons struck you as looking very much like some officers whom you had seen at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: However, two years later, in 1998, you testified in the Dokmanovic case where you failed to mention this at all. You never mentioned Panic, Mrksic or actually recognising any of them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember if anyone asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That's all right. But they did ask yesterday, and you said a thing or two about it. Who are the persons who look like Panic and Mrksic in these photographs? You said that one officer you talked about a while ago and then those three or four others standing nearby?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say who exactly. There was someone looking very much alike, but I can't be positive.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can we agree that there is no way you can have a positive ID, there is no way you can certain that the persons you identified in those photographs were really at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you were told about Panic's photograph they said General Panic. Do we have any other officers called Panic? Was this General Zivota Panic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I heard, General Panic. I didn't know his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. When I asked you about who was on the bus with you, you mentioned Dodaj, and you said that Kuscevic and Hrkic were on a different bus, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: On page 5529 of his testimony Dodaj says that both Kuscevic and were on the bus with him and with you. Do you still stand by your statement or could you perhaps be wrong, or is Dodaj wrong?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: There were a number of other discrepancies, some of which I'm about to point out to you. On 5661, 5663 and 5664 Dodaj says that when you were with him in the group at Ovcara he saw two lieutenant-colonels and another officer who arrived in a Puch. He says they were no other officers there. Is he right or are you right? You have been speaking about three or four officers being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: It's a brief objection just in relation to the method of these questioning, questions, in putting the witness in a position to say whether or not his testimony or another person's testimony is correct. I don't think the witness should be put in that position. I think it's a decision for the Trial Chamber at the end of the day, and it just creates an extra undue influence on the way that the witness may wish to answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You can rephrase that, can you, Mr. Domazet? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zlogledja, let me try to rephrase this. What would you say if I were to tell you that we heard another witness who described this situation and the officers differently, saying that there were only two lieutenant-colonels there and another officer who arrived in a Puch? And you were there together throughout.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he said. I know what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Speaking of Dodaj, we know that you were with him from the beginning to the very end, through all these important situations. I suppose you got close in a way. Do you believe him to be your friend, and did you stay friends after all of this happened?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do see him as a friend, but we haven't really been in touch.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, Mr. Zlogledja, when you were exchanged in the summer of 1992 Dodaj was not with you. He remained in prison to serve out his sentence, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you didn't see him back then. My question is: After 1992, after your return from Valjevo to Croatia, did you ever see him again, did you ever talk to him again?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did meet in The Hague the first time we were here. He was here too, and we met. We met and we talked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I suppose you're talking about the Dokmanovic case, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you ever talk later on, or did you ever phone each other?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did speak on the phone once after that. We were supposed to meet, we were trying to set up a meeting, he was supposed to come over and see me, but he never did, and then we sort of lost touch.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you talk to him about his or your own health, any health problems that you have? Did you speak about that? Did you perhaps talk about that on the phone?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't discuss any health issues. It was more of a general conversation where each of us were, where our families were staying, children, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You considered him a friend back at the time, and you still do. I'm not under the impression that you believe him to be someone who would be inclined to testify against you or to try to put you at some sort of a disadvantage.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you returned to Croatia in mid-1992 -- or rather, you explained to my learned friend a while ago how you gave that statement in 1994. You remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, first of all, you left prison in 1992, and you went back to Croatia. Did you not have any contact at all between 1992 and 1994 with any officials? Did no officials try to approach you and ask you for an interview?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this was the only time that I got a summons for an interview from the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said today that you had an opportunity in The Hague to read that official note and to familiarise yourself with its substance. You did go through it, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The date seems to indicate that this was produced on the 4th of May 1994 in the anti-terrorist squad department of the Zagreb police administration, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you actually remember, or do you want to have a look just to be sure? We can provide a copy if you don't have one. But if you looked at it recently, perhaps you'll remember. There is a detailed description that you provide here, Valjevo, about perhaps going to Slovenia and then finally going to Vukovar and all these persons that you mention here. Do you remember all of that being in that statement?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: There is also a detailed explanation of how you escaped and what you did later on in Vukovar until the surrender. However, what you just said, what you testified in chief, is absolutely correct also. Not a single word about Ovcara in this statement. Not a single word about anything happening there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When I say nothing at all about Ovcara, about you seeing someone there, officers, or anyone else, about them passing through Ovcara, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The substance of this official note is you were captured and were then taken to Negoslavci and then to Belgrade, and then you went on to explain what exactly happened to you, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At the very end of this official note -- okay, this is the quote and you can tell me if that's all right. That you said that you had tried and done your best to remember all the details regarding the events that the interview was about, but you were sure, you said at the time, that you must have forgotten some of the details because of all the time that had elapsed. Also, because you were trying to repress this in order to be able to get on with your life. Did you perhaps state anything like that to the person taking the interview?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may as well have said something like that, but the gist of the interview, I looked at it, I just couldn't believe my eyes. I saw names there that I am sure I had never mentioned and about this time at the Vukovar barracks. It's just that some of these bits don't tally at all. They just don't tie in. I would never have said these things to anyone. Nor would I have omitted the most important details.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you remember being at Ovcara and providing details about this, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Fair enough. Am I to take your answer, this, now, to mean this: That certainly you spoke about Ovcara and what happened at Ovcara to this official of the police administration?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the way the interview was conducted, it had to be the case. It was about life and death. It was important for me to mention that. I couldn't possibly have left that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. However, we do agree that really this is not in the official note. But there is a lot of insubstantial detail about your movements before and after. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I want to know about this too. You said that certain names were included that you didn't know about. I see the names of your colleagues, ones which you have confirmed. Could these be the names of other Croat prisoners being mentioned here that you never mentioned as seeing?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. There are certain names there, first names, that I knew, but there are also surnames that I had never heard before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, but we can agree that if you talked about what had occurred at Ovcara that really, in relation to these details in this official note, was a lot more important, wasn't it, while it doesn't say that what do you think is the reason that this was in the official note. Do you think this was a deliberate move on somebody's part, or do you think this could just be a coincidence that that isn't mentioned here at all?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it's deliberate or not. What I do know is I was shocked when I looked at this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you were shocked. Do you then believe that the police administration could have only omitted it on purpose from this official note?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is clear that this is not in the official note. Now, as to whether they did it on purpose or this was an honest mistake, I don't know, it's their business. I don't know what was in their mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you don't know of any reason for them to do this?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: After that, and up until 1996, did you give any other statements to any officials? When I say 1996, I'm referring to the interview with the OTP.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except for them, I never spoke to anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And then you testified in the Dokmanovic case in early 1998, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ZLOGLEDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I would like to remind you of several pages from the Dokmanovic transcript. I would like to establish whether that is consistent with what you told us now. On page 652, back then in 1998, you described what you saw at Ovcara. You were then asked about the total number, and you answered that there were about 30 people.
